cards.q: Describe the structure of an atom.
cards.a: A small, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in shells.
cards.why: Almost all the mass is in the nucleus; most of the atom’s volume is the space the electrons occupy.

cards.q: Give the relative mass and relative charge of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
cards.a:
Proton: mass 1, charge +1.
Neutron: mass 1, charge 0.
Electron: mass \(\frac{1}{1840}\), charge −1.
cards.why: An electron’s mass is so small it is usually taken as negligible.

cards.q: Outline how the model of the atom developed from Dalton to Bohr.
cards.a:
Dalton: atoms are solid, indivisible spheres.
Thomson: electrons embedded in a sphere of positive charge (plum pudding).
Rutherford: a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with electrons around it.
Bohr: electrons in fixed energy levels (shells).
cards.why: Each model was replaced when new evidence (the electron, alpha-particle scattering, emission spectra) could not be explained.

cards.q: Define atomic (proton) number, \(Z\), and mass number, \(A\).
cards.a:
\(Z\): the number of protons in the nucleus.
\(A\): the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
cards.why: Neutrons \(= A - Z\).

cards.q: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in \({}^{34}_{16}\mathrm{S}^{2-}\)?
cards.a: 16 protons, 18 neutrons, 18 electrons
cards.why: A negative charge means electrons gained; a positive charge means electrons lost.

cards.q: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in \({}^{56}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\)?
cards.a: 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 23 electrons
cards.why: The charge changes only the number of electrons, never the nucleus.

cards.q: What are isotopes?
cards.a: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
cards.why: So isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

cards.q: Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties but can have different physical properties.
cards.a: Chemistry depends on electrons; physical properties such as density depend on mass.
marks: Isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same electron configuration.
Chemical reactions involve electrons, so the chemical properties are the same.
Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons, so different masses.
Properties that depend on mass, such as density and rate of diffusion, can differ.

cards.q: Define relative isotopic mass.
cards.a: The mass of an atom of an isotope compared with \(\frac{1}{12}\) of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
cards.why: Carbon-12 is the standard: it has a relative isotopic mass of exactly 12.

cards.q: Define relative atomic mass, \(A_{\text{r}}\).
cards.a: The weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared with \(\frac{1}{12}\) of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
cards.why: Weighted mean: it takes account of the abundance of each isotope.

cards.q: When should “relative formula mass” be used instead of “relative molecular mass”?
cards.a: For compounds with giant structures, such as ionic compounds like \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), which are not made of molecules.
cards.why: Both are found the same way: add up the relative atomic masses in the formula.

cards.q: Name the stages of a time of flight (TOF) mass spectrometer, in order.
cards.a: Ionisation, acceleration, ion drift, ion detection, then data analysis.
cards.why: Ions are made, given the same kinetic energy, separated by how fast they travel, then counted.

cards.q: Describe how a sample is ionised by electrospray ionisation.
cards.a: The sample is dissolved in a volatile solvent and forced through a fine hollow needle held at a high positive voltage. Each molecule gains a proton, forming \(\mathrm{XH^{+}}\) ions.
cards.why: Electrospray causes little fragmentation, so it is used for larger molecules.

cards.q: Write the equation for electrospray ionisation of a molecule \(\mathrm{X}\).
cards.a: \(\mathrm{X(g) + H^{+} \rightarrow XH^{+}(g)}\)
cards.why: The ion detected has a mass one unit greater than \(\mathrm{X}\), so \(M_{\text{r}}\) is the \(m/z\) value minus 1.

cards.q: Describe how a sample is ionised by electron impact ionisation.
cards.a: The sample is vaporised and bombarded with high-energy electrons from an electron gun, which knock an electron off each particle, forming \(\mathrm{X^{+}}\) ions.
cards.why: Electron impact is used for elements and compounds of low relative molecular mass; it causes fragmentation.

cards.q: Write the equation for electron impact ionisation of an atom \(\mathrm{X}\).
cards.a: \(\mathrm{X(g) + e^{-} \rightarrow X^{+}(g) + 2e^{-}}\)
cards.why: The fast electron is still there afterwards, along with the one it knocked off.

cards.q: Explain how ions of different mass are separated in a TOF mass spectrometer.
cards.a: Lighter ions travel faster, so they reach the detector first.
marks: Positive ions are accelerated by an electric field so that all have the same kinetic energy.
Since \(KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}\), ions with smaller mass have greater speed.
In the drift region, lighter ions travel faster and take less time to reach the detector.

cards.q: How are ions detected in a TOF mass spectrometer?
cards.a: Each positive ion gains an electron at the detector, which produces a current. The size of the current is proportional to the abundance of that ion.
cards.why: The time of flight gives \(m/z\); the current gives relative abundance.

cards.q: Ions of \({}^{24}\mathrm{Mg}^{+}\) are accelerated to a kinetic energy of \(2.00 \times 10^{-16}\ \text{J}\) and travel along a \(1.50\ \text{m}\) flight tube. Calculate the time of flight. (\(L = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(1.50 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{s}\)
cards.why: Convert the mass of one ion to kilograms before using the kinetic energy equation.

cards.q: Boron is 19.9% boron-10 and 80.1% boron-11. Calculate its relative atomic mass to one decimal place.
cards.a: 10.8
cards.why: The answer must lie between the isotope masses, nearer the more abundant one.

cards.q: A mass spectrum of magnesium shows peaks at \(m/z\) 24, 25 and 26 with relative abundances 78.6, 10.1 and 11.3. Calculate \(A_{\text{r}}\) to one decimal place.
cards.a: 24.3
cards.why: Always divide by the total abundance, which is not always 100.

cards.q: Copper has \(A_{\text{r}} = 63.55\) and two isotopes, copper-63 and copper-65. Calculate the percentage abundance of copper-63.
cards.a: 72.5%
steps: Let the fraction of copper-63 be \(x\); copper-65 is then \(1 - x\).
cards.why: Working backwards from a relative atomic mass needs only the isotope masses.

cards.q: Chlorine is 75% \({}^{35}\mathrm{Cl}\) and 25% \({}^{37}\mathrm{Cl}\). Predict the molecular ion peaks for \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\) and their relative heights.
cards.a: Peaks at \(m/z\) 70, 72 and 74 in the ratio 9 : 6 : 1.

cards.q: How can a mass spectrum be used to identify an element, and to find the relative molecular mass of a compound?
cards.a:
An element: calculate \(A_{\text{r}}\) from the isotope peaks and match it to the Periodic Table.
A compound: the molecular ion peak, \(\mathrm{M^{+}}\), with the greatest \(m/z\) gives \(M_{\text{r}}\).
cards.why: With electrospray ionisation the ion is MH⁺, so subtract 1.

cards.q: Define first ionisation energy.
cards.a: The energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
cards.why: The “gaseous” is essential: forget it and the mark is lost.

cards.q: Write the equation for the first ionisation energy of sodium.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Na(g) \rightarrow Na^{+}(g) + e^{-}}\)
cards.why: Include state symbols: every species is a gas.

cards.q: Write the equation for the second ionisation energy of magnesium.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Mg^{+}(g) \rightarrow Mg^{2+}(g) + e^{-}}\)
cards.why: A successive ionisation energy removes one more electron from the gaseous ion, not two electrons from the atom.

cards.q: State the three factors that affect the size of an ionisation energy.
cards.a: Nuclear charge, distance of the electron from the nucleus, and shielding.
marks: Nuclear charge: more protons attract the electron more strongly.
Distance: an electron further from the nucleus (in a higher shell or sub-shell) is held less strongly.
Shielding: inner electrons repel the outer electron and reduce the attraction it feels.

cards.q: Explain the general increase in first ionisation energy across Period 3.
cards.a: The nuclear charge increases while the shielding stays about the same.
marks: The number of protons (nuclear charge) increases across the period.
Electrons are added to the same shell, so shielding is similar.
Atomic radius decreases, so the outer electron is held more strongly.

cards.q: Explain why first ionisation energy decreases down Group 2.
cards.a: The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded.
marks: Each element has an extra shell of electrons.
The outer electron is further from the nucleus.
There is more shielding from inner shells.
This outweighs the increase in nuclear charge, so the outer electron is held less strongly.

cards.q: Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium.
cards.a: Aluminium’s outer electron is in a higher-energy 3p sub-shell.
marks: Aluminium’s outer electron is in the \(\mathrm{3p}\) sub-shell; magnesium’s is in \(\mathrm{3s}\).
The \(\mathrm{3p}\) electron is higher in energy and slightly further from the nucleus.
It is partly shielded by the \(\mathrm{3s}\) electrons, so less energy is needed to remove it.

cards.q: Explain why the first ionisation energy of sulfur is lower than that of phosphorus.
cards.a: Sulfur’s outer electron is in a 3p orbital that already holds another electron.
marks: Phosphorus has three unpaired \(\mathrm{3p}\) electrons; sulfur has one pair in a \(\mathrm{3p}\) orbital.
The two paired electrons in the same orbital repel each other.
So less energy is needed to remove one of them.

cards.q: The successive ionisation energies of an element show a large jump between the third and fourth. Which group is the element in, and why?
cards.a: Group 13 (3). The fourth electron is removed from a shell closer to the nucleus.
cards.why: Three electrons are in the outer shell; the big jump marks the start of a new, inner shell with much less shielding.

cards.q: Explain why successive ionisation energies of an element always increase, even within the same shell.
cards.a: Each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion.
marks: After each electron is removed, the same number of protons attracts fewer electrons.
There is less repulsion between the remaining electrons, so the ion is smaller.
The next electron is held more strongly, so more energy is needed.

cards.q: How do atomic emission spectra provide evidence for quantum shells?
cards.a: They are made of separate lines, not a continuous spectrum. Each line is light of one frequency, emitted when an electron falls from a higher energy level to a lower one.
cards.why: Only certain energy differences are possible, so electrons can only have fixed energies: shells.

cards.q: How many electrons can the first four quantum shells hold?
cards.why: Shell \(n\) holds \(2n^{2}\) electrons.

cards.q: What is an orbital?
cards.a: A region within an atom that can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins.
cards.why: Each sub-shell is made of orbitals: one in s, three in p, five in d.

cards.q: Describe the shapes of an s orbital and a p orbital.
cards.a: An s orbital is spherical. A p orbital is dumbbell-shaped.
cards.why: The three p orbitals in a sub-shell lie at right angles to each other.

cards.q: How many electrons can an s, a p and a d sub-shell hold?
cards.why: Two electrons per orbital: one s orbital, three p orbitals, five d orbitals.

cards.q: How do electrons fill the orbitals of a sub-shell?
cards.a: They occupy the orbitals singly before pairing up, and two electrons in the same orbital have opposite spins.
cards.why: So nitrogen’s three \(\mathrm{2p}\) electrons are in three separate orbitals.

cards.q: Write the full electron configuration of iron (Z = 26).
steps: After \(\mathrm{3p^{6}}\) (18 electrons), \(\mathrm{4s^{2}}\) takes 2 more, leaving 6 for \(\mathrm{3d}\).
cards.why: The \(\mathrm{4s}\) sub-shell fills before \(\mathrm{3d}\) because it is lower in energy.

cards.q: Write the electron configurations of chromium and copper, and say what is unusual about them.
cards.why: Only one electron is in \(\mathrm{4s}\): a half-filled or filled \(\mathrm{3d}\) sub-shell is more stable.

cards.q: Write the electron configuration of \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\).
steps: Remove the two \(\mathrm{4s}\) electrons first, then one \(\mathrm{3d}\) electron.
cards.why: When a transition metal forms an ion, the \(\mathrm{4s}\) electrons are lost before the \(\mathrm{3d}\).

cards.q: Write the electron configuration of the sulfide ion, \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\).
steps: Add two electrons to the \(\mathrm{3p}\) sub-shell: \(\mathrm{3p^{6}}\).
cards.why: The sulfide ion has the same configuration as argon.

cards.q: How is an element classified as s-, p- or d-block?
cards.a: By the sub-shell that its highest-energy electron occupies.
cards.why: Groups 1 and 2 are the s-block, Groups 13 to 18 the p-block, and the transition elements the d-block.

cards.q: Why do elements in the same group have similar chemical properties?
cards.a: They have the same number of electrons in their outer sub-shells (the same outer electron configuration).
cards.why: Reactions involve the outer electrons, so the electron configuration determines the chemistry.

cards.q: True or false: because 4s fills before 3d, a transition metal loses its 3d electrons first when it forms an ion.
cards.a: False. The 4s electrons are lost first.
cards.why: Once \(\mathrm{3d}\) is occupied, \(\mathrm{4s}\) is higher in energy, so its electrons are removed first.

cards.q: True or false: first ionisation energy is the energy to remove an electron from an atom.
cards.a: Incomplete. It is per mole, and the atoms must be gaseous.
cards.why: One mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms, forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
